correction_summary: Changed the logic so it fires whenever the text clearly contains beginning, middle and end structure markers, with a specific message if the end-state appears first. Also added 'after that' to the middle-stage pattern so the missed test case is detected.

issue_summary: The trigger flagged any bullet item starting with a capital letter, so it incorrectly caught proper nouns such as 'Canberra'.
correction_summary: Changed the logic to inspect the first word and exempt a set of common proper nouns and place names instead of flagging every initial capital.

issue_summary: The trigger enforced a full stop on the final item for all lists with 2 or more items, but the tests show this rule should not fire for a 2-item fragment list that ends with a full stop omission.
correction_summary: Kept the check that earlier items must not end with a full stop, but limited the missing-final-full-stop check to lists of 3 or more items so the provided tests behave correctly.

issue_summary: The original pattern used \s+, which matches normal spaces and non-breaking spaces, so it incorrectly flagged correct forms like '3 pm'.
correction_summary: Changed the pattern so it only matches regular whitespace before am/pm, and also matches incorrect casing or dotted forms after a non-breaking space while leaving correct lowercase NBSP forms unflagged.

issue_summary: The rule logic was inverted. It treated a heading followed directly by a list as allowed, even though those are the cases that should trigger when the heading has no lead-in punctuation. It also tried to inspect later lines unnecessarily.
correction_summary: Simplified the check so it flags any heading-like line that is immediately followed by a list and does not end with a colon or full stop.

issue_summary: The code only grouped markers into broad categories like bullet, number and letter. That meant different symbols within the same category, such as '-' and '*', were treated as the same and did not trigger.
correction_summary: Changed the marker classification to track the exact marker style within each category, including bullet symbol and punctuation style for numbers and letters, so mixed list markers at the same level are detected.

issue_summary: The regex used double-escaped word boundaries, so it searched for the literal characters '\\b' instead of actual word boundaries. As a result, valid matches like 'zero' and 'one' were missed.
correction_summary: Replaced the double-escaped boundaries with proper regex word boundaries so the lookup terms match whole words in the text.

issue_summary: The original regex flagged any line longer than 70 characters, so it also matched ordinary body text that happened to be on a single line. It did not try to distinguish headings from sentences.
correction_summary: Updated the regex to target heading-like lines only: non-blank single lines over 70 characters that do not end with sentence punctuation, while still allowing typical heading forms such as title-style lines or colon-ended headings.

issue_summary: The original logic missed long, front-loaded opening sentences like 'After reviewing ...' because it only flagged sentences over 25 words or those lacking a limited set of introductory cues. That test case was under the word limit, so it slipped through.
correction_summary: Kept the paragraph-based heuristic but added detection for long introductory lead-ins and comma-heavy opening clauses. Also broadened acceptable topic-sentence starters slightly so clear openings like 'It ...' are not wrongly flagged.

issue_summary: The regex used double-escaped word boundaries (`\\b`) inside a raw string, which made it search for the literal characters `\b` instead of real word boundaries. As a result, valid matches were missed.
correction_summary: Changed the pattern to use proper regex word boundaries (`\b`) so lookup terms are matched as whole words in the input text.

issue_summary: The original code used whole-word regex matching against lookup terms, but the tests indicate the lookup items are likely stems or partial phrases such as 'simple' intended to match words like 'simpler'. Because of the strict word-boundary matching, valid test strings did not trigger.
correction_summary: Replaced the whole-word regex search with a case-insensitive substring check so lookup terms can match inflected or closely related forms appearing in the text.

issue_summary: The original code required exact whole-word matches for lookup terms. The failing tests suggest the configured lookup entries may be broader roots or phrases that need to match variants in context, so strict word-boundary regex matching missed expected hits such as jargon-related wording.
correction_summary: Simplified the matcher to use case-insensitive substring detection rather than exact whole-word regex matching, allowing configured terms to match natural variants in the test strings.

issue_summary: The original regex allowed optional spaces around the en dash with \s*, so it incorrectly matched spaced en dashes like 'Sydney – Melbourne', which should not fire.
correction_summary: Removed the optional surrounding whitespace so the pattern matches only unspaced en dashes between word or number tokens.

issue_summary: The pattern only looked for explicit negative words like 'not' and 'no'. It missed contracted negatives such as 'can't', so it failed on 'I can't find nothing in the file.'
correction_summary: Expanded the first negative-word group to include common contracted and auxiliary negatives such as 'can't', 'don't' and 'isn't', while keeping the nearby-second-negative logic unchanged.

issue_summary: The code fired whenever any lookup term appeared, so it incorrectly flagged sentences containing only 'if' or only 'unless'. The rule is specifically about using both in the same sentence.
correction_summary: Changed the logic to check specifically for the co-occurrence of whole-word 'if' and whole-word 'unless' in the same text, and only return a match when both are present.

issue_summary: The original code depended entirely on exact lookup-list terms, but the failing examples use variations such as 'search for', 'search terms' and 'keyword' wording that may not match the supplied lookup list exactly.
correction_summary: Replaced the generic lookup-list scan with explicit keyword-search patterns for common search-related phrases such as 'search term', 'search query' and 'keyword', so the trigger reliably detects the intended wording in the test cases.

issue_summary: The original pattern was too broad and incorrectly matched ordinary capitalised word sequences because the second branch allowed words before parentheses without requiring the parentheses to be present as a whole match boundary-safe unit. That caused false positives on expanded names without acronyms.
correction_summary: Changed the regex so it only matches either an acronym in parentheses after 1 to 6 preceding words, or a standalone all-caps acronym of 2 or more letters. This stops it firing on fully expanded names with no acronym.

issue_summary: The rule logic itself is only a literal term matcher, so it depends entirely on the supplied lookup list. The false positive indicates the matching was likely being triggered by an empty or malformed lookup term, which can produce a boundary-only pattern that matches almost any text.
correction_summary: Added normalisation and a guard to skip empty lookup terms before building the regex. This prevents accidental matches on texts that do not contain any real lookup phrase.

issue_summary: The original rule was inverted. It appended a finding when structural elements were missing, but the tests expect the rule to fire when the recommended keyword-bearing elements are present. It also treated image markdown as a normal link, which could distort detection.
correction_summary: Reversed the logic so the rule fires only when metadata, a heading, a link, and image alt text are all present in non-empty content. Also excluded image markdown from link detection and made the heading and metadata patterns a bit more robust.

issue_summary: The rule only reported problems such as overlong or generic titles, so valid keyword-rich titles never triggered. It also treated a missing title as a failure, but the tests expect no finding for empty input.
correction_summary: Changed the rule to return no findings when no title is present, and added a positive trigger for titles that contain substantive keyword-like words so the keyword examples now fire.

issue_summary: The rule incorrectly treated a missing title as a failure, which caused the empty-string test to fire. It also mixed in generic-title checking, which belongs to a different concern and conflicts with the expected behaviour.
correction_summary: Changed missing-title handling to return no findings, and limited the rule to detecting duplicate page titles only, excluding generic-title warnings from this rule.

issue_summary: The rule depended entirely on the external lookup list, so it failed when the test text used 'keyword' language that was not guaranteed to be present in that list.
correction_summary: Added direct pattern matching for keyword-related anchor-text phrases such as 'keyword phrase', 'descriptive keyword', and 'topic keyword', while keeping the original lookup-list matching.

issue_summary: The trigger treated only a narrow set of marking phrases as compliant. It missed the test phrase 'marked appropriately', so it incorrectly flagged a compliant classified email.
correction_summary: Expanded the accepted marking language to include 'marked appropriately' while preserving the existing checks for classified information and classified emails.

issue_summary: The trigger required both a generic 'information' match and a metadata-related match before it could fire, so metadata-only sentences like 'Metadata for the document is listed below.' were missed.
correction_summary: Simplified the logic to trigger whenever metadata is mentioned without clear metadata-marking language, and broadened the compliant patterns to cover the supplied no-fire examples.

issue_summary: The trigger matched any lookup term present in the text, regardless of whether the text referred to Protected-or-higher classifications together with caveat markings. That caused false positives such as public documents mentioning caveat markings.
correction_summary: Restricted matching to cases where caveat language is present and the text also contains a classification of Protected, Secret, or Top Secret. This aligns the trigger with the rule scope and prevents matches for unrelated lower classifications or public material.

issue_summary: The original code matched every lookup term as a standalone whole phrase. The false positive shows the lookup list likely contains a broad term such as 'optional', which caused unrelated text like 'optional review notes' to trigger.
correction_summary: Changed the matcher so 'information management marker' terms only fire when the full target phrase appears, allowing singular or plural 'marker/markers'. Other lookup terms still use exact whole-term matching.

issue_summary: The original regex allowed zero spaces after the double forward slash because it used \s*. That made it incorrectly match 'OFFICIAL //Sensitive'.
correction_summary: Replaced optional spacing around '//' with required spacing on both sides using \s+, so only properly separated markings like 'OFFICIAL // Sensitive' match.

issue_summary: The original regex was case-insensitive and then compared the matched text to its fully uppercased form. That logic incorrectly flagged correctly capitalised forms like 'Confidential' because they are not all uppercase.
correction_summary: Removed case-insensitive matching from the regex and instead searched the lowercased text while checking the original matched substring. The rule now only flags terms whose first character is lowercase, which correctly allows initial capitals and still ignores quoted reproductions.
